object detection, segmentation, and keypoint prediction to recover the 6D pose of known objects through
Perspective-𝑛-Point. Starting from synthetic training, DOPER adapts to real observations using partial
supervision while retaining synthetic keypoint labels. Calibrated multi-view observations provide geometric
constraints for keypoint supervision. During inference, optional heatmap refinement fits a rigid pose directly
to the predicted keypoint distributions, resolving ambiguous correspondences without depth input or a
learned pose refiner. Starting from underspecified CAD models, DOPER progressively refines the object
representation and pose estimator. Results on SPEED+ and SHIRT further demonstrate effective adaptation
to illumination changes and accurate temporal pose estimation. Across the evaluated single-view and multi-
view configurations, DOPER achieves state-of-the-art

Overview and problem formulation.DOPER
combines synthetic supervision and real observations
to adapt an object-specific pose estimator (Figure 2).
Given a calibrated RGB image, an approximate CAD
model, and ordered object-frame keypoints, we esti-
mate object rotation and translation relative to the
camera. The CAD appearance and surface details
may be incomplete, but metric scale must be known.
Keypoint identities and their coordinate frame remain
fixed throughout adaptation.
Shared visual representation and geometric
pose estimation.Following the correspondence-
based formulation of DOPE [60], we predict image
locations of known object points and recover pose
with P𝑛P. Our implementation shares a DINOv3-
pretrained ConvNeXt backbone [53] between a full-
image branch and an object-crop branch. The full-
image branch combines multi-scale features at stride
four and predicts object

centers, bounding-box di-
mensions, center offsets, and a foreground mask. De-
tection follows the CenterNet formulation [76]. For
each detected box, the crop branch resamples the
original image at higher resolution and applies the
same backbone weights, followed by a keypoint head.
This preserves small-object detail while sharing de-
tection and segmentation supervision with keypoint
localization. The head predicts a spatial distribu-
tion per keypoint; decoded coordinates are mapped
to the original image by the inverse crop transform.
Confidence filtering and robust P𝑛P select consistent
2D–3D correspondences and minimize squared repro-
jection error, accounting for camera calibration and
lens distortion.

To test whether real observations can compensate
for CAD deficiencies, we remove texture or part of
the geometry from 19 HANDAL objects (Figure 8).
We reconstruct the objects from onboarding videos
with NuRec [42] and replace half of the synthetic
training images with NuRec composites. Compared
with matched composites of the degraded CAD model,

and 16.3 points in the two settings, respectively.
These gains are consistent across most objects; Ap-
pendix B details the training protocol, statistical anal-
ysis, and results.

evidence.excerpt:
We present DOPER, which learns detection and key-
points jointly and uses geometric fitting to estimate
object pose. The same keypoints support multi-view
estimation and heatmap refinement, while synthetic
initialization and partial real supervision enable adap-
tation. DOPER achieves strong RGB results across
four object-pose benchmarks and supports illumina-
tion adaptation and temporal pose estimation on
SPEED+ and SHIRT. Our HANDAL study further
shows that reconstructions from onboarding videos
can compensate for missing texture and incomplete
CAD geometry.
These results leave several challenges open: reduc-
ing per-object training and refinement costs, and mak-
ing reconstruction-based adaptation independent of
annotated poses. Furthermore, a universal metric key-
point detector could help streamline object onboard-
ing and reduce reliance on object-specific training
data

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Headline results are measured with ground-truth annotations and standardized BOP test protocols, independent of the self-training signals used for adaptation.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Ground-truth pose error metrics on official held-out benchmarks: BOP MSSD/MSPD AP, SPEED+ rotation/translation error, and SHIRT trajectory tracking errors.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Supervised losses on synthetic domain-randomized renders combined with self-training adaptation signals: SAM-generated masks, coarse orientation consistency, and multi-view triangulated keypoint reprojection on unannotated real observations.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Reported experimental results support the claims of achieving competitive state-of-the-art performance across tested benchmarks and demonstrating clear benefits from adaptation and heatmap refinement.
primary.evaluation_assessment: The system is evaluated extensively across standardized BOP benchmarks (HANDAL, HOPEv2, HOT3D, T-LESS) as well as orbital tracking benchmarks (SPEED+, SHIRT). Evaluations include standard BOP detection AP (MSSD and MSPD) on official test/validation sets, ablation studies on keypoint placement and count, runtime profiling, and CAD degradation recovery using 3D reconstructions.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Evaluations rely on independent ground-truth annotations and standardized BOP challenge test protocols rather than self-supervised adaptation scores.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Standard ground-truth pose error metrics (BOP MSSD/MSPD AP, SPEED+ rotation/translation error, and SHIRT trajectory tracking errors) computed on official held-out test and validation benchmarks.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Supervised loss on synthetic domain-randomized renders combined with self-training adaptation losses (SAM-generated masks, coarse orientation consistency, and multi-view triangulated keypoint reprojection) on unannotated real scenes.

primary.limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge limitations including the requirement of known metric scale, per-object training and refinement overhead, dependence on annotated poses for reconstruction-based onboarding, and reliance on approximate CAD models.
primary.method_assessment: The architecture shares a DINOv3 ConvNeXt backbone across a full-image detection branch and a high-resolution crop keypoint branch, trained with mixed synthetic domain randomization and partially supervised real observations. Multi-view calibration and optional non-linear heatmap refinement are clearly formulated to resolve pose ambiguities geometrically without requiring learned depth-based refiners.
primary.quality_rationale: The methodology is thoroughly documented, technically sound, and evaluated against established baselines and official challenge benchmarks with granular ablations, meeting the standard for admission.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper introduces DOPER, a framework that jointly learns 2D object detection, segmentation masks, and 3D keypoint heatmaps for 6D pose estimation via PnP, coupled with test-time adaptation strategies using monocular pseudo-labels and multi-view geometric constraints.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The methodology is thoroughly documented, technically sound, and evaluated against established baselines and official challenge benchmarks with granular ablations, meeting the standard for admission.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The authors explicitly acknowledge limitations including the requirement of known metric scale, per-object training and refinement overhead, dependence on annotated poses for reconstruction-based onboarding, and reliance on approximate CAD models.
